verdicts.why: Names an accusation in plain words; the offence is the referent, and the word takes no side on whether the accusation is fair.
Custody or care as a plain fact; 'the charge of her' says who is responsible without approving or belittling anyone.
A ward, the person in one's care; a role-word like 'pupil' or 'patient' with no attitude attached.
Strong meaning, not attitude: it says the emotion was overwhelming, and the irony in 'fatigued with the raptures of his wife' comes from 'fatigued', not from the word.
Intense joy named as a state; a learner choosing it over 'delight' is saying the joy was greater, not that they think better or worse of it.
Bad referent, plain word: it reports that hopes were not met without blaming or pitying either party.
Power to sway, stated neutrally; 'boundless influence' can be admired or feared depending on context, and the word itself does neither.
The effect of one thing on another; a causal description with no judgement built in.
A person who has sway over another; the label names the relation and says nothing about whether the sway is good.
Reports whose affection someone holds ('a great favourite with her nieces'); the warmth belongs to the people described, not to the speaker's choice of word.
'Her favourite walk' states a preference as a fact; the word describes a ranking without the speaker judging the thing ranked.
The competitor expected to win; a betting term with no attitude toward the competitor.
Plain purchase; nothing distinguishes it in attitude from 'purchase' except register.
Chosen over 'believe' it casts the claim as a sales pitch and its believer as a possible dupe ('she bought his story'); sceptical, faintly dismissive of what is accepted.
A compliment word: to call something elegant is to approve of its taste, which is why Mr. Bennet's 'such an elegance to misfortune' works as irony; approving.
In science and mathematics an 'elegant' solution is high praise, not a neutral description of its shape; admiring.
Greeting on arrival, done cordially or not ('not welcomed home very cordially'); the word names the act and the manner is supplied separately.
Accepting gladly describes the acceptor's own attitude as a fact; the speaker who uses it is reporting, not judging.
Receiving someone into one's house; a plain hospitality verb with no attitude beyond its meaning.
